strengths: Broad, systematic empirical sweep: 15 LLMs across 5 families and 3 openness levels, 3 survey datasets (WGM, OQA, WVS), and 3 distribution-elicitation methods, with results reported for all models in the appendix. This is a genuinely large experimental effort.

The distribution-level framing is appropriate: evaluating elicited answer distributions (rather than majority-voted responses) against human response distributions via a Wasserstein-based opinion-alignment metric is a sensible extension of prior work and better matches the pluralistic-alignment goal the authors invoke.

The calibration results are consistent and clearly reported: supervised regression improves alignment in the large majority of dataset-model-elicitation settings and reduces both within-setting and cross-setting variance, with per-demographic breakdowns (Tables 6-8) that constitute a useful empirical resource.

Additional analyses add value beyond the headline result: data efficiency (as few as ~5 gold examples suffice), out-of-domain generalization (Appendix A.5), log-probability elicitation (Appendix A.3), and the OLMo post-training comparison (SFT/DPO/RLVR) are informative and somewhat unusual in this literature.

Reproducibility is reasonable: prompts for base and sociodemographic conditions are given verbatim (Tables 12-13), demographics are listed (Table 11), and the authors state they open-source code and outputs. Limitations and an ethics discussion (including the risk of essentializing demographic groups) are included.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The distributional elicitation setup and the opinion-alignment metric are taken from Santurkar et al. (2023), and the negative result that sociodemographic prompting does not consistently help replicates Beck et al. (2024) and Hu and Collier (2024) in a non-distributional setting. The genuinely new component is a per-answer-choice supervised regression (simple, univariate, with normalization) — essentially a light calibration layer.

The headline "16.3% average improvement" is not defined in the main text and appears to be an average of per-setting *relative* improvements, which is inflated by low-baseline settings (e.g., WVS paraphrase 59.6 -> 80.5). The aggregate absolute improvement in Table 1 is much smaller (e.g., verbalized averages ~83.4 -> ~86.1, roughly 3 points). The paper should define the metric precisely and foreground absolute alignment values.

Practical circularity / weak utility claim. The regression is trained and evaluated within the same dataset (60-20-20 split over questions and demographics), so applying it to new questions requires in-dataset gold human distributions — the very quantity being predicted. The most decision-relevant evidence (train on two datasets, test on a third; Tables 9-10) shows much smaller gains (e.g., WGM verbalized 84.6 -> 85.3) and is buried in Appendix A.5. The utility claim should be scoped to "calibration with a pilot set of human responses," not general prediction of human opinion.

Underpowered per-demographic claims. The study uses only 92 questions (WGM 14, OQA 38, WVS 40) with 4-6 examples per demographic. The authors acknowledge low significance but still advance directional claims (RQ3, Section 6.2, e.g., which demographic groups benefit or degrade most). These claims are not statistically supported and should be softened or given proper uncertainty quantification.

The "LLMs exaggerate differences between sociodemographic groups" conclusion (Section 9) rests mainly on reduced variance after calibration. Variance reduction is a mechanical consequence of any regression/shrinkage and does not by itself demonstrate exaggeration. A model-free comparison of inter-group dispersion in LLM vs. human distributions (before calibration) would be needed to support this claim.

Metric and statistical reporting issues. Normalization of 1 - Wasserstein is not fully specified, ground-truth group distributions have varying and often small sample sizes with no uncertainty estimates, the paired-test/Bonferroni "significance" bolding is fragile with 14-38 questions, and alignment values are compared across datasets with different answer scales and question types as if commensurable.

Narrow elicitation space and unablated design choices. Chain-of-thought, in-context examples, and fine-tuning are excluded (acknowledged), temperature is fixed at 0.7, and n = 3 (verbalized) vs. n = 5 (self-random/paraphrase) is not ablated, which limits the generality of the "verbalized elicitation is best" conclusion that several later analyses depend on.

Presentation. The main text is organized as five RQs with hedged "it depends on model, dataset, and elicitation method" conclusions, making it hard to extract a crisp takeaway; the practical guidance in Section 8 largely restates limitations rather than offering a validated recipe.

strengths: Broad and systematic empirical study: three large survey datasets, 15 LLMs, three distribution-elicitation methods, and multiple demographic categories, yielding a useful benchmark for distributional opinion alignment.
Important negative finding: sociodemographic prompting does not consistently improve alignment with human response distributions, challenging a common assumption and providing practical guidance.
Simple supervised calibration substantially improves alignment on average (16.3%) and reduces variance across settings, with as few as 5 supervised examples often sufficient.
Uses an ordinal-aware Wasserstein-based opinion alignment metric, which is appropriate for Likert-scale survey data and more suitable than KL/Jensen-Shannon divergences for this setting.
Group-level analysis adds nuance by showing which demographics benefit from calibration and how alignment varies across models, datasets, and sociodemographic groups.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed prompt templates, model/dataset specifications, and appendices with extensive additional results; the work is also stated to be open-sourced.
Thoughtful ethical framing, including discussion of essentializing demographics and limitations, which is important for this line of work.
Clear research questions and practical suggestions for practitioners, making the empirical findings actionable.
weaknesses: The calibration approach is a supervised regression trained per dataset-LLM-elicitation setting using ground-truth human distributions. No baseline compares against predicting question-level human marginals or against standard calibration methods (e.g., temperature scaling, histogram matching, isotonic regression), so it is unclear whether the gains come from leveraging LLM signal or from shrinkage/mean reversion.

Methodological novelty is limited: the core technique is a straightforward regression calibration, and the contribution is primarily empirical. This makes main-conference consideration borderline despite the breadth of the study.

The evaluation uses only 92 unique questions (14 WGM, 38 OQA, 40 WVS), and per-demographic sample sizes are often 4-6 examples. Group-level conclusions (RQ3/RQ4) therefore have low statistical power, and the paper reports few significant differences.

Calibration models are setting-specific and must be retrained for each new dataset, model, and elicitation method, limiting practical generality. Out-of-domain generalization is tested only across the three included datasets and is modest.

The main results table bolds many pairwise differences, but the statistical testing procedure for the headline calibration gains is not fully specified (e.g., multiple-comparison correction, confidence intervals), making some aggregate claims harder to assess rigorously.
RQ5 on post-training effects is limited to the OLMo model family, so conclusions about SFT/DPO/RLVR effects may not generalize to other model families.

No exploration of chain-of-thought or other stronger prompting strategies, and temperature/sample sizes are fixed at relatively small values; this could affect the elicitation quality and the reported comparisons.

The paper does not compare calibrated LLM distributions against a human-agreement ceiling or annotator noise ceiling, so it is difficult to know how close the calibrated predictions are to the practical upper bound.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: aligning LLM-generated response distributions with diverse human populations, moving beyond majority-answer sociodemographic prompting.
Extensive empirical study across 3 survey datasets (WGM, OQA, WVS), 15 LLMs of varying openness/size/post-training, and 3 distribution elicitation methods, with 220,500 generated distributions.

Clear and well-supported negative result: adding sociodemographic information to prompts does not consistently improve distributional alignment; effectiveness is model, dataset, and elicitation-method dependent.
Supervised calibration is simple and effective: it improves opinion alignment in 94.8% of settings by 16.3% on average, and reduces variance across examples and settings.
Includes useful analyses of demographic-level variation, data efficiency (as few as 5 examples can suffice), out-of-domain generalization, and effects of post-training.
Paper is generally well-written, with prompts and extensive per-demographic results in the appendix, supporting transparency and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The calibration method is a global per-answer-choice regression and cannot adapt to question-specific content or demographic interactions; it may improve alignment largely by shrinking distributions toward marginal human answer distributions rather than correcting question-level errors.

The main text does not fully specify the train/dev/test split for calibration (whether held-out questions are disjoint at the question level) and lacks details on how regression examples are sampled, making the supervision setup hard to assess.

No code or data release link is provided despite claiming open-sourcing; exact implementation details (hyperparameter ranges, random seeds, significance testing procedure for Table 1) are insufficient for full reproducibility.

Ground-truth human distributions for some demographic groups may be estimated from small survey subsamples; uncertainty in these targets is not propagated into the alignment metric or statistical tests, potentially inflating apparent demographic differences.

Calibration is compared only against uncalibrated prompting baselines, not against alternative calibration approaches (e.g., temperature scaling, vector scaling, or other distribution alignment methods), so the strength of the calibration contribution is unclear.
The main text reports only the most powerful model per family, which may overstate average performance; although the appendix contains all models, the main claims rely on a subset.

The regression objective optimizes MSE on answer-choice probabilities rather than the Wasserstein-based alignment metric, which may be suboptimal and could explain why calibration is less effective in some settings.
The paper acknowledges but does not deeply address the risk that calibration can degrade alignment for some sociodemographic groups, especially those historically less represented.

strengths: Broad and systematic empirical study spanning 3 survey datasets, 15 LLMs, 3 distribution-elicitation methods, 2 prompt categories, and extensive appendices, which supports reproducibility and gives the findings credibility.
A clear and useful negative result: sociodemographic prompting does not consistently improve alignment with human response distributions, which challenges common assumptions in prior work.

A positive and well-supported result: supervised calibration improves distributional alignment by a sizable margin on average and substantially reduces variance across datasets, models, and elicitation methods.
Demonstrates that calibration can work with minimal supervision (1-10 examples) and shows out-of-domain generalization to unseen datasets, increasing practical relevance.

Uses an ordinal-aware alignment metric based on normalized Wasserstein distance, reports significance tests with correction, and includes limitations, ethical considerations, and demographic-level analysis.
The paper is well motivated by pluralistic alignment and the ecological fallacy, and the benchmark/prompt release can stimulate future work on distributional alignment.
weaknesses: The core method is a straightforward regression trained on human response distributions; its technical novelty is limited, and it is not compared against strong alternative baselines such as directly predicting human marginals per question, temperature scaling, or prior distributional calibration methods.

The train/test split is ambiguous and potentially leaky: it is not made fully clear whether splits are by question or by question-sociodemographic group. If the same question appears in both train and test under different demographic groups, the calibration model may exploit question-specific human distributions and inflate alignment.

Calibration requires human survey labels from the target setting (dataset, LLM, elicitation method, prompt type), so it is not a zero-shot alignment solution; the paper does not fully analyze the practical cost or the consequences of using unrepresentative human supervision.

The paper reports average improvements but gives limited analysis of when and why calibration fails (the 5.2% of degrading settings) and whether gains reflect meaningful alignment rather than artifacts of the metric.

Some claims, such as calibration 'greatly' improving alignment, are stronger than the evidence presented; effect sizes and confidence intervals are not consistently reported, and practical significance beyond statistical significance is not fully established.

Comparisons to related distributional elicitation and calibration work are limited, and the analysis does not sufficiently separate the contribution of LLM-generated information from simply learning the human answer distribution for each question.

strengths: Broad, well-executed empirical study: 3 survey datasets, 15 models (open-source, open-weight, API), 3 elicitation methods, and 2 prompt categories, yielding 270 settings and large numbers of elicited distributions.

Reproducibility is a genuine strength: full prompt templates for base, sociodemographic, few-shot, and CoT variants are provided (Tables 14-16), models are named, and the pipeline is described in enough detail to reimplement.

The negative result on sociodemographic prompting is useful as a large-scale, distributional replication: SD prompting does not consistently improve alignment and often hurts, which is a valuable confirmation across many models/datasets/elicitation methods.
The paper reports out-of-domain generalization (Appendix A.4) and post-training effects (Sec. 7), adding breadth beyond the headline claim.
The Limitations and Ethical Considerations sections are candid about demographic essentialization and the risks of the method.
weaknesses: The central claim — that supervised calibration improves alignment — is close to tautological. The regression is fit to human ground-truth distributions for the same questions and demographic groups (with held-out splits), so improvement in the alignment metric is essentially guaranteed by the construction. This is not a substantive discovery about LLMs, yet it is framed as the paper's main contribution (the '16.3% improvement' headline).

The variance-reduction result and the inference drawn from it ('LLMs exaggerate differences between sociodemographic groups, which calibration might mitigate') are confounded by regression's inherent shrinkage. A model trained to predict a target will reduce variance across settings by construction; this is a property of the estimator, not evidence about model behavior, and it should not be presented as such.

Limited novelty. The finding that sociodemographic prompting does not consistently improve alignment is already well documented (Beck et al., 2024; Santurkar et al., 2023; Hu & Collier, 2024; Mukherjee et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025b). The calibration method is a simple element-wise regression closely related to Cao et al. (2025) and Meister et al. (2025). The paper's framing overstates how new either element is.

The calibration mechanism is not well characterized. The regression takes only the LLM's per-answer-choice values as input (no question or group features) and predicts each choice independently before renormalizing. It is unclear whether it learns a global recalibration or something question-specific, and the 'few examples suffice' result (Sec. 6.1) suggests a very simple transformation — which undercuts the framing of calibration as a meaningful correction rather than a trivial rescaling.

The few-shot comparison in Sec. 6.2 is not apples-to-apples. The few-shot examples also include human response distributions (i.e., supervision), so comparing 5-shot prompting to a trained regression does not cleanly test whether calibration 'learns something useful.' Additionally, only 3 random samples are used, which is a weak basis for the stated conclusion.

The per-demographic analyses (Sec. 5.1, Sec. 6.3; Tables 3, 5) are underpowered: by the authors' own admission there are only 4-6 examples per group and none of the differences are statistically significant. Conclusions drawn from these percentages (e.g., which models align best with which regions, or which groups degrade most) are therefore not well supported.

The claim of providing a 'benchmark' is overstated. The work is an elicitation-and-calibration pipeline applied to existing survey datasets, not a new benchmark dataset; the abstract's framing implies a resource contribution that is not delivered.

A practical and conceptual tension is left unresolved: calibration necessarily improves alignment for some groups while degrading it for others (the paper acknowledges this), which directly undermines the pluralistic-alignment motivation. The paper does not quantify or systematically analyze this trade-off, even though it is central to whether the method is desirable.

Presentation is dense and hard to parse (e.g., Table 1 mixes significance bolding with yellow/blue best-value highlighting across many column pairs), and the headline 16.3% figure aggregates over heterogeneous settings without clarifying what the transformation is actually doing.

strengths: The paper conducts a comprehensive empirical study spanning 3 survey datasets, 15 LLMs, 3 distribution elicitation methods, and multiple prompting strategies, yielding a large-scale benchmark for distributional alignment.

It provides clear evidence that sociodemographic prompting does not consistently improve distributional alignment, while simple supervised calibration improves alignment by 16.3% on average across 94.8% of settings and reduces variance across models and elicitation methods.
The finding that 1-10 supervised examples suffice for calibration is practically useful and is compared against few-shot prompting, showing calibration's greater consistency.
Reproducibility is strong: prompts, dataset details, model versions, and an open-source benchmark are provided, and the analysis includes sociodemographic and post-training variations.
weaknesses: The central method—supervised regression calibration—is technically straightforward, and the main improvement is largely expected because the regression is trained on human response distributions from the same datasets; the novelty is more empirical than methodological.

Main calibration results appear to rely on a single 80/10/10 split per setting without reporting variance across splits or confidence intervals, and several datasets contain few questions, which may make the reported gains sensitive to the particular split.
The per-answer-choice regression does not enforce ordinal or non-negativity constraints; renormalization after regression could produce invalid or distorted distributions, and this is not analyzed.

The study does not compare against alternative calibration approaches (e.g., isotonic regression, Dirichlet calibration, or directly fine-tuned distribution predictors), so it is unclear whether the proposed regression is the most effective or efficient choice.
Individual sociodemographic analyses often lack statistical significance due to small per-group samples, limiting the strength of conclusions about which groups are better or worse aligned.

The calibration requires in-domain human distribution labels for training questions and only tests out-of-domain generalization in the appendix; it is therefore not a general alignment solution and may not transfer to new surveys or domains without additional supervision.
